sixRules.intro: Every score in this guide assumes you follow these first. None of the materials on the scorecard can rescue a garment you wear five times and throw away.

rules.title: Wear it thirty times, at least
rules.text: Impact is counted per wear, not per garment. This one habit outweighs every fibre choice in this guide.

rules.title: Buy one fibre, never a blend
rules.text: Pure cotton and pure polyester can each be recycled. Poly-cotton cannot be separated. Some stretch clothes really do need elastane, but most shirts and jeans do not.

rules.title: Buy secondhand first
rules.text: A used garment carries zero new production impact. It is the largest saving available to you, and it costs less.

rules.title: Wash cold, full loads, air dry
rules.text: Most of a garment's lifetime energy is spent after you buy it, not before.

rules.title: Repair before you replace
rules.text: A re-stitched hem, a new zip, a resoled shoe. Each one buys years for a fraction of the price.

rules.title: Read the fibre tag, not the ad
rules.text: "Eco", "natural", "bamboo" and "vegan" are marketing words. The composition label is what actually tells you what you're buying.

wearStats.note: The entire cost of making a garment is carried by five wearings. This is the fast-fashion default.
Impact per wear drops sharply every time you put the same garment on again, simply by keeping it longer.
Nothing you can change about the fibre itself comes anywhere close to the effect of wearing a garment out fully.

sixRules.footnote: No fibre is perfect and none is beyond saving. A 9.5 bought carelessly and worn twice still beats nothing, and a 2.0 you already own and wear for a decade is not a failure. Garments sold at retail are generally required to declare fibre composition, so if a seller won't tell you the mix, that itself is a signal.

microplastics.intro: Plastic microfibre is far too small for any household or municipal filter to catch. Once it leaves your wash water it is gone for good, so reducing it at the source is the only lever that exists.
worse: Fleece, brushed and fluffy surfaces — loose fibre ends are what break off; smooth, tightly woven synthetics shed far less
Hot water and long wash cycles — heat and agitation time both raise fibre loss
Half-empty wash drums — less fabric means more free movement and more abrasion per garment
The first few washes of a new synthetic garment — it sheds most when new
Tumble drying — sheds fibre a second time, into the air, on top of the energy it burns
better: Wash synthetics less often — air them out instead
Cold water, short cycle, full load
Air dry rather than tumble dry
A filter bag or drum filter for synthetics you already own, catching a meaningful share
Buy fewer new synthetics where you genuinely have a choice — nothing else here has as much effect

journey.text: Abrasion in the drum breaks loose fibre ends off the fabric surface.
Fibres leave with the greywater. No household filter catches them.
Wastewater treatment removes some. What passes through reaches open water.
Fish, salt and drinking water all carry measurable microplastic.
Microplastic has been found in human blood, lungs and placenta. It does not leave the body.

stats.label: Microfibres released by a single six-kilo acrylic wash load in lab testing.
The warming potency of nitrous oxide released during nylon production, compared to CO2.

beforeYouBuy: Check the fibre composition tag before you look at the price
Prefer durable, single-fibre materials where practical
Consider how often you will actually wear the garment
Avoid unnecessary blends when you have a choice
tagCheck: Find the composition tag before you look at the price
One fibre if you can — two or more usually means it can never be recycled
Elastane is fine in socks and activewear, which need the stretch; worth skipping in shirts, denim and bedsheets, which don't
Acrylic and wool are not the same word — check which one the label actually says
Ask about certification if you're paying an organic or recycled premium
Then ask the real question: will I wear this thirty times?

endOfLife.title: Repair
endOfLife.text: A hem, a zip, a seam or a sole costs a fraction of replacement and buys years.

endOfLife.title: Pass on
endOfLife.text: Family, friends, a resale platform. Someone else's wear counts too.

endOfLife.title: Repurpose
endOfLife.text: Cotton becomes cleaning cloth, patchwork or quilt filling.

endOfLife.title: Recycle last
endOfLife.text: Single-fibre garments only — which is exactly why buying one fibre at a time matters.

wordsThatMeanNothing.meaning: Almost always viscose. The word names the raw material, not the process that actually determined its footprint.
Usually PVC or PU. "Vegan" is an animal-welfare claim, not an environmental one.
Unregulated marketing words with no standard, audit or fixed meaning behind them.
Viscose and modal both start as plants. The phrase says nothing about the chemistry or water used to process them.
Pure what? A composition percentage is the only statement that actually binds a seller.

marksThatMeanSomething.meaning: Global Organic Textile Standard — the most widely recognised organic claim, covering the farm and every processing step after it.
Plain Woolmark means all-new wool. Woolmark Blend and Wool Blend mean progressively less of it.
Global Recycled Standard — verifies recycled-content claims, including recycled polyester, and always names a certifying body.

ifYouChangeOneThing: Choose single-fibre garments where you reasonably can, and don't throw out synthetic clothing you already own just to replace it. Replacing a working polyester shirt with a new cotton one makes things worse, not better — wear it out first.
sourcesAndMethod: Fabric scores and descriptions are adapted from The Fabric Scorecard, a public guide summarising published life-cycle assessment literature on textile fibres (comparative LCAs of cotton, polyester, viscose and lyocell; microfibre shedding studies; and textile industry fibre data). Brand information is compiled from official brand websites and public reporting where available, and is clearly marked where it reflects a brand's own claim rather than independent verification.

fastFashion.intro: Fast fashion is not a single company or fibre — it is a pattern: trend cycles that turn over quickly, prices low enough to encourage buying more than needed, and garments that get worn only a handful of times before being replaced rather than repaired.
points: Rapidly changing trends encourage frequent purchases rather than long-term use.
Low-cost mass production makes replacing a garment cheaper, in the moment, than repairing it.
Garments worn only a few times carry the same production footprint as one worn for years — the difference is entirely in how long it stays in use.
Synthetic fibres add a second cost at the washing stage: shedding microplastic fibres that wastewater treatment cannot fully catch.
Disposal culture — treating clothing as short-lived rather than durable — shifts the problem to landfill and informal waste streams rather than solving it.
fastFashion.note: This section reflects the wear-multiplier data and the six rules from the source scorecard rather than external fast-fashion statistics, to avoid citing figures that could not be verified for this project.
